Or was there other things going on? Or -- doesn't look like there's a whole lot of seasonality in the business because last year's fourth quarter, I'm talking fourth quarter of 2022 was pretty strong. So just any more color on the likeliness in orders in the fourth quarter of '23?
David G. Anderson
President of Air & Liquid Systems Corporation, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
Yes, I can do that. The Buffalo Air certainly, as I talked about, was one of the impacts. The other one Buffalo Pumps was light in the fourth quarter, which happens sometimes when you're dealing with government contracts, sometimes they want to get them placed or don't. While that was slower in the fourth quarter, we saw it pick right back up in January and February. So I think that for pumps, it was just a timing issue. For Buffalo Air, it's an issue of a bit of a product of our success in bookings that we have simply sold out a lot of more capacity.
Dennis J. Scannell
Principal & Portfolio Manager, Rutabaga Capital Management LLC
Yes. Okay. Great. And then just for clarity, the the grant from the U.S. Navy for manufacturing equipment, is that for additive manufacturing? Or is it for a different process?
David G. Anderson
President of Air & Liquid Systems Corporation, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
It's for a different process. These are CNC machines. This is separate from the funding they provided for the additive work we're doing with them.
Dennis J. Scannell
Principal & Portfolio Manager, Rutabaga Capital Management LLC
Got it. Okay. Great. And then just Mike, thinking about cash flow for 2024, it was very helpful. The first questioner on kind of separating out the maintenance cap spending because that [ 15 to 20 ] was a lot higher than I had been [indiscernible]
Michael G. McAuley
Senior VP, Treasurer & CFO, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
Sorry about that.
Dennis J. Scannell
Principal & Portfolio Manager, Rutabaga Capital Management LLC
No worries. [indiscernible] sharp in draw breath, but I feel better now. But for 2024, it's going to be higher than that 10 to 11. I'm guessing we have $4 million left in the Forged businesses capital program. So would we expect it closer to 15 or 16? Or am I being too pessimistic there?
Michael G. McAuley
Senior VP, Treasurer & CFO, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
Well, first of all, we're probably going to spend about $18.5 million on the Forged and Cast Modernization Program from out the full 20. That's one piece. On the -- we're going to -- that's how much we're going to use on the equipment financing facility. So that's one piece and it's funded. So yes, we will have CapEx, our original business plan was something in the range of $10 million, $11 million. It might reap a little higher than that, but it's going to be -- it's not going to be much higher than that, and it's definitely a big step down from 2023 where we had a lot of the spending going on for the major program.
Dennis J. Scannell
Principal & Portfolio Manager, Rutabaga Capital Management LLC
Absolutely. No, that's great. And working capital, would you think that would be a source of cash and in '24, particularly kind of no growth on the roll business?
Michael G. McAuley
Senior VP, Treasurer & CFO, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
That's kind of the -- yes, that's kind of the thought process for the construction of our 2024 outlook is that we're expecting that working capital doesn't at least provide additional pressure. -- in terms of cash flow from operating [indiscernible]. .
Dennis J. Scannell
Principal & Portfolio Manager, Rutabaga Capital Management LLC
Great. And then just one last thing. And I know on the asbestos issue and I know these calculations are really -- are very complicated. But just looking at your reported results, we talked about the cost per [indiscernible], it's actually gone down. It was like 22,000 in 2020 and 2021. In 2023, it was under 19,000. And -- just kind of curious, the -- but the actuaries or whoever are doing these calculations are saying, no, we're expecting that to go higher going forward?
Michael G. McAuley
Senior VP, Treasurer & CFO, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
Yes, usually done. That's a very good question, Den. But usually, we don't do revaluations every year. We do them every couple, several years. because you hate to jump and do a whole revaluation and then suddenly things change in variables and some of the most sensitive -- the most sensitive variables in the entire valuation [indiscernible] settlement values and the claim mix. And those are the two things that have caused the increase here. If you think about when we did the last valuation a few years ago, we were looking at a rolling average that pulled in multiple years prior to the current data. And those values were more in the range of 14, 15-ish kind of numbers. And now that they've stepped up, that's kind of the rationale.
Operator
And this concludes our question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the conference back over to Brett McBrayer for any closing remarks.
J. Brett McBrayer
CEO & Director, Ampco-Pittsburgh Corporation
I continue to be encouraged by our strengthening operational performance as we were to mitigate the headwinds in our European Cast roll business, we are very optimistic with the opportunities we see for stronger financial performance moving forward. I want to thank our employees for the tremendous hard work and dedication to the business. We've done an outstanding job and continuing to do so. I also want to thank our shareholders. Thank you for joining our call this morning.
Operator
Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. We thank you all for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect your lines, and have a wonderful day.
